entities.name: Marcus Antonius Primus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Antonius Primus (c. 30 CE – after 98 CE) was a pivotal Roman senator and military commander whose decisive actions in 69 CE fundamentally altered the succession of the Roman Empire. Originating from Tolosa (modern Toulouse), he rose to prominence during the tumultuous Year of the Four Emperors, a period of civil war that erupted following Nero's suicide. His strategic brilliance and willingness to challenge established authority directly led to the collapse of Emperor Vitellius's regime and paved the way for the Flavian dynasty under Vespasian, thereby stabilizing an empire on the brink of prolonged chaos. He embodied the opportunistic yet capable military leadership that often dictated imperial power during times of instability.

Initially exiled during Nero's reign for fraud, Antonius Primus was recalled by Galba and given command of Legio VII Galbiana in Pannonia. After Galba's assassination and Otho's brief rule, he quickly aligned with Vespasian, who was then commanding forces in Judaea. In autumn 69 CE, defying Vespasian's explicit orders to await his arrival, Primus led the Danubian legions (Legio VII Galbiana, Legio XIII Gemina, Legio XI Claudia) across the Alps into Italy. He achieved a crushing victory over Vitellius's forces at the Second Battle of Bedriacum, near Cremona, a brutal engagement that saw an estimated 30,000 casualties. Following this, he marched on Rome, overcoming fierce resistance and ultimately capturing the city in December 69 CE, a move that culminated in Vitellius's brutal death and the proclamation of Vespasian as emperor.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marcus Antonius Primus's decisive military victories in 69 CE directly installed the Flavian dynasty, which provided decades of stability to the Roman Empire after a period of civil war. His actions demonstrated the critical role of military power in shaping imperial succession, setting a precedent for future Roman history.
